analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil company excess profits and uses the money for transit fare cuts and fuel-efficient car credits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: introduced May 4, 2005 with 51 cosponsors, it was sent to two committees and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a tax on oil and gas company profits above a level a new federal board judged "reasonable" — with rates rising from 50% to 100% of the excess. The money would fund two things for ordinary people: tax credits of up to $6,000 for buying fuel-efficient cars built in America by union workers, and federal grants letting bus and commuter rail systems cut their fares. It was referred to two House committees, sent to a transportation subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Commuters and drivers facing high gas prices would get cheaper bus and rail fares and credits toward efficient American-made cars; mass transit agencies would get federal money to cut fares; union-represented U.S. auto plants would gain demand for qualifying vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commuters, drivers, transit riders, union auto plants

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on oil and gas sales equal to 50% of profits above a board-determined "reasonable" level, rising to 75% and then 100% of the excess as profits climb further past it.

Creates a tax credit of $3,000 to $6,000 for buying fuel-efficient passenger vehicles assembled in the United States by workers under collective bargaining agreements, with bigger credits for higher mileage.
Authorizes the Transportation Secretary to make grants to bus and commuter rail operators to reduce fares, applied equally to all passengers.
Funds the transit fare reductions with the windfall tax revenue, after paying for the car credit.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and refiners would pay the windfall tax; buyers of vehicles that do not meet the fuel-economy or union-assembly requirements would get nothing; taxpayers generally fund the new Reasonable Profits Board.

drawbacks.text: A windfall profits tax on oil sales could be passed along to consumers at the pump, raising the very gas prices the bill targets — the classic objection to this kind of tax, last tried in the 1980s.
The bill relies on a three-member presidentially appointed board to define "reasonable profit," an open-ended judgment call that invites years of litigation and administrative dispute.
The car credit is restricted to vehicles assembled in the U.S. under collective bargaining agreements, excluding imports and non-union plants and limiting consumer choice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets high gas prices at the source — oil company profits — and recycles the revenue into cheaper transit fares and efficient-car credits, a coherent trade. Its real weaknesses are design ones: the pump pass-through risk, the difficulty of defining reasonable profit, and a car credit narrow enough to exclude most vehicles on the lot.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Transportation committees, sent to a transit subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on May 4, 2005, during a period of rising gas prices, with 33 original cosponsors.
It gathered 51 cosponsors in total, all Democrats or the one Independent, and none were Republicans.

The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; the Transportation committee sent it to its Highways, Transit and Pipelines subcommittee on May 5, 2005.
No committee ever reported it out; the sponsor made additional introductory remarks in September 2005 and May 2006, but the bill sat until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies avoided the windfall tax, and drivers and transit riders got none of the fare relief or car credits it offered.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor three times over 2005 and 2006.

for.name: 50 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making its support entirely from one party.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral for the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the 21 months after referral.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to its Highways, Transit and Pipelines subcommittee, where it stayed without further action.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican supported it, and the House was under Republican control in the 109th Congress.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would tax up to 100% of their profits above a board-determined reasonable level, directly hitting the industry's earnings during price spikes. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against drivers' interest in relief at the pump.
The car credit required U.S. assembly under a collective bargaining agreement, channeling buyer demand toward union plants. The buy-American design was a deliberate boost for domestic union labor.
Vehicles assembled in the U.S. without a union contract, and imports, would not qualify for the credit, putting them at a disadvantage against union-built competitors.
Bus and commuter rail systems would receive federal grants to cut fares, boosting ridership at cheaper prices for passengers.
